sentences.text: Morrosaurus antarcticus was a medium-sized, herbivorous dinosaur that lived in Antarctica during the late Cretaceous. The single known specimen is estimated to be between 4.5 and 5 meters in length.
This animal was larger and more robust than its relative Trinisaura, which measured only 1.5 meters.

Two unique derived traits were identified in the bones: the inferior view of the greater femoral trochanter has a wavy profile with a thick exit edge and a thin main edge, while the fourth metatarsal bone has a triangular profile with a backward-pointing projection that wraps around it and the third metatarsal. On the femur, the lesser trochanter is inclined diagonally, right next to the greater trochanter, and on the tibia, the medial malleolus has a triangular outline and shows a concave anterior surface.
The greater trochanter of Morrosaurus forms an S-shape in bottom view, a trait seen in other elasmarians but more extreme in this species.
Members of the Elasmaria group, including Morrosaurus, show adaptations for a high-speed running lifestyle indicated by a narrow foot with a thin fourth metatarsal.
Laterally expanded chevrons are associated with a larger surface for anchoring lateral tail muscles, providing good control of tail movements.
A curved humerus demonstrates the absence of a deltopectoral crest, meaning the front limb was not used for walking.
A partial skeleton of a euornithopod was discovered in Antarctica in 2002 by paleontologist Fernando Novas.
The species Morrosaurus antarcticus was named and described in 2016 by a team including Sebastian Rozadilla and Fernando Novas, though some sources cite the description year as 2015.
The genus name Morrosaurus refers to the fossil site of El Morro on James Ross Island.
The species name refers to Antarctica.
The holotype specimen MACN Pv 197 was found in the Snow Hill Island Formation at Cape Lambe and dates to the Maastrichtian age.
The known remains consist of a right hind leg, including parts of the femur, tibia, foot, and the first joint of the third toe.
Morrosaurus antarcticus is the only known species of the extinct elasmarian ornithopod dinosaur genus Morrosaurus.
The interrupted rapid growth strategy of Morrosaurus was likely an adaptation to the varying resource availability in Antarctica.
The close relationship between Antarctic Morrosaurus and South American elasmarians demonstrates faunal links between these continents.
Morrosaurus is classified within Iguanodontia as a basal member of Euiguanodontia.
Morrosaurus belongs to the clade Elasmaria, which includes ornithopods from Patagonia and Antarctica such as Trinisaura and Gasparinisaura.
Morrosaurus lived during the Maastrichtian age of the late Cretaceous period, specifically from 72.2 to 66 million years ago, in the area of modern Antarctica.

It is debated whether Morrosaurus possessed the specific running adaptations of the Elasmaria clade due to the fragmentary nature of the fossil remains, and it cannot be determined whether Morrosaurus itself possessed these characteristics due to its limited remains.
